title: Bacon Chop with Parsley Sauce
subtitle: Thick-cut cured pork with a classic parsley butter sauce
excerpt: A bacon chop is a thick steak cut from the back of the pig, cured like back bacon but substantial enough to pan-fry as a main course. Parsley sauce, a simple white sauce finished with plenty of chopped flat-leaf parsley, is the traditional British accompaniment that makes the combination complete.
sourceNotes: Bacon chops with parsley sauce appear in British farmhouse cookery throughout the twentieth century. Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), Project Gutenberg #10136, documents both boiled bacon and parsley sauce as standard British preparations. The combination is a fixture of school dinners and traditional British pubs.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The parsley sauce can be made up to 30 minutes ahead. Keep warm over a very low heat, stirring occasionally, and add a splash of milk if it thickens too much.

content.text: A bacon chop is a thick slice cut from the back of the pig, cured like a rasher but four or five times as thick. It has enough substance to hold its own as a main course, where a standard rasher would disappear. Parsley sauce is a simple white sauce made with butter, flour, and milk, finished with a generous amount of finely chopped parsley. The sharpness of the parsley cuts through the salt and fat of the bacon.

items.prepNote: bacon chops, about 200 g each and 2 cm thick

content.text: Melt {{unsalted-butter}} of butter in a small saucepan over a medium heat. Add {{plain-flour}} of flour and stir with a wooden spoon for 1 to 2 minutes until the mixture forms a smooth paste and smells biscuity but not raw.

Remove from the heat and pour in a quarter of the {{whole-milk}}, whisking constantly until smooth. Return to a medium heat and gradually add the remaining milk, whisking between each addition. Bring gently to a simmer, stirring, and cook for 3 to 4 minutes until the sauce has thickened and lost its floury taste.
Stir in the {{parsley-flat}} of chopped parsley and season with a pinch of salt and pepper. Keep warm over the lowest heat while you cook the bacon chops.
Cook the bacon chops and serve

Pat the bacon chops dry with kitchen paper. Heat {{olive-oil}} of oil in a frying pan over a medium-high heat until shimmering. Add the chops and cook for 6 to 7 minutes on the first side without moving them, until deep golden brown underneath. Turn and cook for a further 5 to 6 minutes.
Rest the chops on a warm plate for 5 minutes. Serve with the parsley sauce poured over, alongside mashed potato or boiled new potatoes.

items.cause: The milk was added too quickly, or the roux was too hot when the milk went in.
items.fix: Remove from the heat before adding the first splash of milk and whisk vigorously. If lumps persist, pass through a sieve and return to the heat.

items.cause: The sauce was cooked too long or the heat was too high.
items.fix: Add a splash of warm milk and whisk in over a low heat until the consistency loosens. The sauce should coat the back of a spoon but pour easily.

items.symptom: The bacon chop is too salty
items.cause: Bacon chops are cured and can be quite salty, especially smoked ones.
items.fix: Soak the chops in cold water for 30 minutes before cooking to draw out some of the cure. Pat dry before frying.

items.symptom: The bacon chop is dry in the centre
items.cause: The chop was overcooked or sliced too thin.
items.fix: A 2 cm chop needs about 12 to 14 minutes total over medium heat. Use an instant-read thermometer; the centre should reach 68°C. Rest before cutting to let the juices settle.

content.text: Bacon chops with parsley sauce are a school-dinner and pub-lunch staple that dates back through British farmhouse cooking. Parsley sauce was the default white sauce in Victorian and Edwardian kitchens: cheap to make, flavoured with whatever herb was growing by the kitchen door. The dish is particularly good alongside boiled or mashed potatoes and buttered peas. It fell out of fashion as food culture moved toward the Mediterranean in the 1990s, but has a loyal following among those who ate it as children.
